title: Akavya ben Mahalalel

paragraphs: In [Mishnah Eduyot 5:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Eduyot.5.6), he testified to four rulings. He regarded “reserved hair” and green blood as ritually impure, whereas the sages regarded them as pure.[^1] He permitted the use of hair that had fallen from a blemished firstborn animal, been placed in a window, and been followed by the animal’s slaughter; the sages prohibited it. He said that neither a female convert nor a freed female slave is given the water to drink; the sages said that they are.[^2] They told him of Karkemit, a freed female slave in Jerusalem whom Shemaya and Avtalyon had given the water to drink. He answered: “They gave her the drink because she was like them.”[^3] The sages told him: “Retract the four rulings you have maintained, and we will appoint you av bet din for Israel.” He replied: “Better that I be called a fool all my days than become wicked before the Omnipresent for even one hour, lest people say: ‘He retracted for the sake of power.’”

These rulings also appear individually in their respective places: [Niddah 2:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Niddah.2.6), [Bekhorot 3:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Bekhorot.3.4), and [Negaim 5:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Negaim.5.3).

He is also mentioned in [Negaim 1:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Negaim.1.4): Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas says that there are thirty-six appearances of skin lesions; Akavya ben Mahalalel says seventy-two. (It seems that there is no disagreement here. Rather, he was so expert in the appearances of skin lesions that he could distinguish seventy-two different appearances from one another. His opinion is listed last because the enumeration proceeds from the smaller number to the larger.)

His cherished saying has also come down to us at the beginning of [Avot, chapter 3](https://www.sefaria.org/Pirkei_Avot.3.1): “Consider three things, and you will not come to sin. Know where you came from—from a putrid drop; where you are going—to a place of dust, maggots, and worms; and before whom you will have to give an account and a reckoning—before the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He.”

Now we know with certainty that Akavya lived after Shemaya and Avtalyon. But how long after them? The view expressed in [*Darkhei ha-Mishnah*, page 56](https://hebrewbooks.org/pdfpager.aspx?req=31828&pgnum=63), is that he lived close to the time of Hillel and Shammai, and that after Shammai’s death they wished to appoint him av bet din. The author’s reasoning is that Akavya lived before disagreement had broken out, when no individual was heard stating a ruling on his own; Akavya dared to do so, and therefore they told him: “Retract.” That concludes the quotation. But this scholar forgot that we already find Shammai and Hillel disagreeing with the sages on several occasions, and [Shabbat 15a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.15a) explicitly records the sages disagreeing with them.
It appears clear, however, that Akavya lived even before Shammai was appointed av bet din, and that when Menachem departed they wished to appoint Akavya.[^4] We shall bring three proofs.

**First:** [Sanhedrin 88a](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.88a) asks why Akavya ben Mahalalel was not executed under the law of the rebellious elder. It is known that forty years before the destruction of the Temple the Sanhedrin ceased to judge capital cases, as stated in [Shabbat 15a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.15a). From this we see that he lived before that time.

**Second:** Their words, “Retract, and we will appoint you av bet din,” show that this was before Shammai’s time. For it is known that after the deaths of Hillel and Shammai the office of av bet din ceased, and only Rabban Gamliel the Elder served as nasi.

**Third:** His words to his son in Eduyot, “I heard it from the many,” suggest that he lived in the time of the sons of Beteira. At that time, the Sanhedrin’s power had been abolished by Herod’s father; only houses of Torah study remained, and the office of nasi was temporarily entrusted to the sons of Beteira. He therefore said: “I heard it from the many.” Later, when the two schools, the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel, had been established, we never find a pupil of either school being told to retract. At that time there were two houses of Torah, equal to one another in standing and stature. The House of Shammai preceded the House of Hillel by a considerable period, as explained in their entries.

In *Mevo ha-Mishnah*, page 271, the author says that one may suggest that Akavya ben Mahalalel lived when Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya was appointed, and that they told Akavya they would choose him as av bet din. He also proposes there that Issi ben Akavya, who lived in Rabbi’s time, was his son. How far this is from the truth! This scholar reasoned that, because Akavya is mentioned in Eduyot and gives testimony there, the whole tractate was taught “on that day.” But he erred: all the testimonies were assembled together then; it does not follow that all the sages mentioned there lived at that time. This is clear.

[Eduyot there](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Eduyot.5.6) relates that they excommunicated him, that he died while excommunicated, and that the court stoned his coffin. Rabbi Yehuda said (in [Sifrei, Beha’alotekha, section 105](https://www.sefaria.org/Sifrei_Bamidbar.105), it is Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, and this is correct): “Heaven forbid that Akavya was excommunicated! No one in Israel entered the Temple courtyard who equaled Akavya ben Mahalalel in wisdom and fear of sin.”[^5]

[At his death](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Eduyot.5.7), he told his son: “Retract the four rulings I maintained. I heard them from the many, and they heard them from the many. I stood by what I had received—but you heard it from an individual.” His son asked his father: “Father, commend me to your colleagues.” He answered: “I will not commend you.” His son said: “Have you found some wrongdoing in me?” He answered: “No. Your deeds will bring you near, and your deeds will keep you far away.”
Perhaps his son’s name was Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya.

notes.text: “Reserved hair” (*se’ar pekudah*) is a technical category of white hair that remains after a skin lesion has disappeared and is present when the lesion returns; see the linked Mishnah in Negaim. “Green” translates Hyman’s *yarok*, a color term whose range in rabbinic usage can also include yellow. These are discussions of ritual status, not modern medical classifications.

The water is the water used in the sotah ordeal, administered to a wife suspected of adultery. Hyman abbreviates the account; explanatory words in the translation identify the ritual without supplying a new historical claim.

The terse expression *dugma hishkuha* admits more than one interpretation; both are recorded in [Bartenura on Eduyot 5:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Bartenura_on_Mishnah_Eduyot.5.6.8). The rendering follows the interpretation that she was like Shemaya and Avtalyon in descent from converts; another interpretation is that they performed only a demonstration of the procedure. Hyman quotes the expression without explaining it, so this interpretation belongs to the translation, not to an explicit explanation by Hyman.

The chronological arguments, assessments of other authors, and proposed identification of Akavya’s son are Hyman’s views. They are translated as his argument, not presented as independently established historical conclusions. *Av bet din* means head of the court; *nasi* denotes its president. “Rabbi,” without a personal name in the passage about Issi, means Rabbi Judah the Patriarch.
His account presents both the report of excommunication and Rabbi Yehuda’s denial. The denial is not silently substituted for the first report.
